architecture.mechanism: Tire elasticity during the shift process smooths vehicle acceleration, reduces oncoming clutch impact, and shortens clutch sliding friction work by extending the engagement time window of the oncoming clutch.
architecture.intervention: Specify or fit tires with controlled (moderate) radial elasticity for the transmission-equipped vehicle, and re-tune the transmission shift schedule (clutch engagement timing/pressure ramp) to extend oncoming clutch engagement time so that the smoother acceleration profile from tire elasticity is preserved, reducing shock loads on clutch and gear synchronizers under low-speed city driving.
architecture.expected_effect: Lower transient impact loads on the transmission's clutches and synchronizers during shifts at ~30 mph, reducing hard-shifting feel, clutch slip, and premature wear/failure even at low total mileage.
architecture.falsification_test: Instrument a test vehicle (or fleet sample) with the modified tire-elasticity/schedule combination and measure shift-event peak clutch impact force, shift duration, clutch slip energy, and shift jerk on a chassis dyno and during repeated 30 mph upshifts/downshifts; compare against baseline stock-tire/schedule results using a paired statistical test (e.g., n≥20 shifts, paired t-test on peak impact and slip work). Failure to show a statistically significant reduction in peak clutch impact and slip work, or any increase in shift harshness, falsifies the mechanism.
